summaries.example: Imagine a sorting game with cards. One rule says, “Every triangle card has three sides.” If you replace “triangle” with another group and the rule stays true, Bolzano would study that pattern. He also asked whether one rule really supports another: from “Every cat is an animal” and “Milo is a cat,” can we reach “Milo is an animal”?
summaries.summary: Bernard Bolzano developed a broad theory of logic and science. He wanted logic to explain how truths are connected and how knowledge should be organized. He distinguished a proposition itself from a person’s act of thinking it and from the sentence used to express it. For him, propositions have truth values, but they do not exist as physical things in time and space. He also treated ideas as parts of propositions. By allowing certain ideas to vary, he could compare whole families of propositions. This led to notions such as universal validity, compatibility, contradiction, and deducibility. Bolzano also connected deduction with conditional probability: certainty and impossibility are extreme cases of a wider measure of how often conclusions hold when premises hold. Finally, his idea of grounding described an objective order among truths, useful for arranging axioms, proofs, and scientific explanations.
key_ideas: Bolzano thought logic should study meanings and their relationships, not just thoughts in people’s minds.
He described propositions as things that are true or false, even though they are not physical objects.
A proposition can be tested by replacing some of its parts with other ideas.
He studied when propositions fit together, when one follows from others, and when they conflict.
He wanted scientific knowledge arranged in an orderly structure, beginning with basic truths.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bolzano’s work shows that logic is not only about memorizing argument rules. It can also ask what statements mean, which changes preserve truth, and how a large body of knowledge can be organized. His ideas helped open paths toward modern studies of meaning, consequence, probability, and axiomatic science.

important_terms.definition: A statement that can be true or false. Bolzano studied the meaning of statements, not only the words or marks used to write them.
A part of a proposition, such as an idea of a person, an animal, or a quality.
A way of changing certain parts of a proposition to see whether its truth stays the same.
A connection in which some true propositions support another truth. Bolzano used this idea when thinking about good scientific explanations.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between a sentence and what that sentence means?
Can a rule be useful even if it is not always true?
When does one statement give a good reason for another?
Why might a science need basic starting points?

summaries.example: Take the form “If every A is B and every B is C, then every A is C.” The letters stand for variable ideas. Bolzano would ask whether every allowed substitution keeps the inference true. He would also distinguish this from a merely factual case such as “Harry Truman was a twentieth-century president, so Harry Truman was not a Buddhist,” which may count as deducible in his broad sense without being a necessary or purely logical connection.
summaries.summary: Bolzano’s logic is part of a larger Theory of Science concerned with the structure, discovery, justification, and presentation of knowledge. Its central innovation is the study of propositions and ideas “in themselves”: objective meanings that are true or false, though not physical or mental events. Ideas are constituents of propositions, and their extensions, contents, and structures help distinguish them. Bolzano analyzes propositions through forms and variation. Once selected parts are treated as variable, one can classify a proposition as universally valid, universally invalid, or intermediate, and can define analyticity as invariance of truth value under an appropriate range of substitutions. He extends analogous extensional relations to groups of propositions. Compatibility means that at least one assignment of ideas makes the relevant propositions true; deducibility means that every assignment verifying the premises verifies the conclusions. This broad relation includes logical cases but also contingent or non-logical connections. Its probabilistic version measures the proportion of premise-supporting variants that also support the conclusion, with incompatibility and deducibility as zero and one limits. Bolzano’s grounding relation is different: it links true propositions in an objective order of explanation, often represented as a hierarchy beginning with basic truths. He presents the theory as tentative in places, but its framework anticipates important questions in semantics, consequence, probability, and axiomatic organization.
key_ideas: Bolzano’s theory of science includes rules for discovering truths, recognizing them, organizing them into disciplines, and presenting them in scientific works.
Logic concerns objective propositions and ideas rather than merely psychological events or linguistic expressions.
The same proposition may belong to several forms because different parts can be selected as variable.
Compatibility is basic in Bolzano’s system; deducibility, equivalence, contradiction, and contrariety are developed from it.
His analyticity concerns invariance of truth or falsity under specified substitutions, so it differs from several later meanings of “analytic.”
Grounding aims to capture explanatory order: a theory should proceed from suitable basic truths while avoiding unnecessary or overly complex premises.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bolzano separates several questions that are often run together: whether a proposition is true, whether it follows from others, whether its truth survives substitution, and whether it explains another truth. These distinctions make arguments and scientific theories easier to examine. They also show why formal logic can be connected with semantics and methodology without reducing every relation to psychology or ordinary language.

important_terms.definition: An objective meaning that is exactly one of true or false, distinguished from a sentence and from someone’s mental judgment.
A constituent of a proposition that is not itself a proposition. Ideas may represent objects, attributes, or logical elements.
A sentential pattern or class of propositions produced by replacing specified parts with permitted substitutes.
A relation between ideas based on their extensions, such as sharing an object, inclusion, equivalence, or exclusion.
Bolzano’s broad relation in which every admissible substitution making the premises true also makes the conclusion true, relative to specified variable ideas.
A relation of support among truths that orders them in a scientific system. It is not identical with deduction or causation.
The proportion of true variants of a conclusion together with the premises to the true variants of the premises alone.

questions_to_think_about: Should logic study meanings independently of thinkers and languages, or only formal expressions?
Does a truth remaining unchanged under substitution make it necessary or knowable a priori? Why might Bolzano separate these ideas?
Why does Bolzano make compatibility a condition of deducibility?
How could a proof be valid yet still redundant?
What would make an argument explanatory rather than merely truth-preserving?

summaries.example: Suppose a club has members numbered 1 through 10. You know that the number chosen is between 1 and 10 and is odd. The conclusion “the number is prime” is true for some, but not all, allowed choices. Bolzano could describe this as having a degree of validity: the conclusion works in three of the four cases that satisfy the two starting statements. If it worked in every case, it would have the strongest possible support relative to those premises.
summaries.summary: Bernard Bolzano developed an ambitious account of logic within his Theory of Science. He saw this larger discipline as concerned with finding truths, recognizing them, dividing them into sciences, and writing well-organized scientific works. At the center is a distinction between propositions in themselves and the sentences or mental judgments connected with them. A proposition in itself is an objective meaning that is true or false but is not a physical object or a mental event. Its parts are ideas in themselves. Bolzano studies these parts by considering forms: selected ideas are treated as variable, and other ideas are substituted for them. A proposition is universally valid when all suitable variants are true, universally invalid when all are false, and neutral when both kinds occur. He calls a proposition analytic when its truth value remains fixed under a suitable variation, a use that differs from Kant’s and later philosophical uses. He also defines relations among propositions. Compatibility requires at least one permitted set of substitutions that makes the propositions true together. Deducibility requires that every substitution verifying the premises verify the conclusion. Because this relation depends on the chosen variables, it is broader than purely logical consequence and can include contingent connections. Bolzano’s conditional probability is based on the ratio of successful conclusion cases to premise cases. Lastly, grounding describes an objective, non-causal order among truths, helping explain how axiomatic sciences may be structured from basic truths and economical proofs.
key_ideas: Bolzano treats logic as part of a larger project: building and organizing the sciences.
He distinguishes objective meanings from sentences, thoughts, and judgments.
Studying forms lets us test what happens when selected ideas are replaced.
Relations among ideas and relations among propositions have parallel structures.
Deducibility is broader than modern-sounding logical consequence because the variable parts are explicitly specified and may include ordinary concepts.
Conditional probability measures how often a conclusion is true among the cases in which the premises are true.
summaries.why_it_matters: Bolzano’s approach gives students a way to see logic as the study of structures of meaning, not just as a collection of symbols. It links deduction, probability, semantics, and scientific explanation while keeping them distinct. His work is historically important because it explores forms of consequence and objective scientific organization before many familiar modern treatments were developed.

important_terms.definition: A meaning that is true or false, unlike the written or spoken sentence that expresses it.
A non-propositional part of a proposition, such as a person, class, property, or logical marker.
A pattern formed by marking some parts of a proposition as replaceable and specifying what may replace them.
A relationship between ideas determined by the objects they represent, including overlap, inclusion, equivalence, and incompatibility.
A relationship where at least one permitted replacement makes all the relevant propositions true together.
A relationship where every permitted replacement that makes the premises true also makes the conclusion true.
An objective support relation among truths, used to arrange a science from basic truths toward results.

questions_to_think_about: If two sentences use different words but express the same meaning, should logic treat them as the same proposition?
Why might the result of an argument depend on which parts we allow to vary?
Can a conclusion follow from a premise without following by necessity?
How is an explanation different from a list of facts?
What makes a starting truth suitable for a scientific system?
